ai.title: How accurate our forecasts are
ai.subtitle: park.fan runs a model of its own, trained on the queues measured at more than 200 parks. It factors in the weather forecast, school holidays and special events, and every day at 06:00 UTC it learns from the previous day’s wait times.
ai.avgErrorDesc: MAE: how many minutes off our predictions are on average
ai.rmseDesc: RMSE: how bad the worst misses are, outliers weighted more
ai.mapeDesc: MAPE: percentage error relative to actual wait time
ai.coverageDesc: of all predictions checked against measurements
ai.r2ScoreDesc: R²: how well the model explains wait time variance
ai.howText: Three things go into every forecast: the park’s measured wait-time history; the weather forecast, school holidays and public holidays; and what is happening at the park that day, such as a special event or the start of the season. From those the model works out the expected wait per ride and per hour and combines them into the day’s crowd level, as far ahead as the park has published its schedule.
ai.improvingTitle: Every forecast is checked the day after
ai.improvingText: The day after a forecast, the system lays it next to the wait time actually measured and writes the difference into the next training run. The figures above come from that comparison.

method.title: Where these numbers come from
method.measured: Every figure on this page comes from measurements. The source is the <posted>posted wait time</posted> published {inPark}: park.fan reads it continuously and files every reading with a timestamp. This analysis covers {days} operating days across {years} years.
method.percentiles: “Typical” is the median of all readings: half the <wait>wait times</wait> were below it, half above. “Peak” is the 90th percentile, the value only one reading in ten went past. The median is what to expect, the peak is what a full day looks like. A month’s <crowd>crowd level</crowd> sums up both across every ride.
method.hourly: The day curve rests on a shorter window: {days} operating days since {from}. Hours in which a ride reported nothing stay empty and don’t count as zero minutes.

faq.whatIsA: park.fan collects live wait times from more than 200 theme parks in 23 countries. Every park page carries the current wait times of its rides, the show times, the opening hours and the crowd calendar for the months ahead.
faq.whichParksQ: Which theme parks are on park.fan?
faq.whichParksA: park.fan covers over 200 theme parks worldwide, among them Phantasialand, Europa-Park, Disneyland Paris, Efteling, Walibi Belgium, Toverland and Bobbejaanland. The full list with live wait times is on the parks overview page.
faq.liveDataQ: Are the wait times on park.fan live and in real-time?
faq.liveDataA: Yes. Wherever a park publishes its wait times, we poll them every five minutes from the sources that list the park, up to three: ThemeParks.wiki, Wartezeiten.app and Queue-Times.com. ThemeParks.wiki is the main source; the other two add rides it lacks and correct a stale “closed” status. The result is rounded to five minutes, because that is how the parks post them.
faq.freeA: Yes. Live wait times, opening hours, shows, restaurants and the crowd calendar are all there without an account and without a paywall. There is no subscription tier with more data behind it.
faq.mobileA: Yes. park.fan runs in the browser on a phone, a tablet or a computer, so there is no app to install. In the park you can use it to see where the queue is short right now. When the site can tell you are inside a park, the nearest rides move to the top.

method.title: How the forecast works
method.summary: Every figure here comes from wait times park.fan measures every five minutes, a forecast built on them, and the hours the parks publish. Open a question for the details.

sources.title: Where do the numbers come from?
sources.body: park.fan records the posted wait of every ride every five minutes. Our forecast models learn from those measurements, the parks' hours, school holidays and the weather. Opening hours, Early Entry and evening events come from the parks' own calendars. We check seasons and parties by hand.

minutes.title: What do the minutes mean?
minutes.body: For each park we forecast the wait at its big rides, each at its busiest time of day, and average them. It is the one number we compare parks by. In the morning and the evening lines are shorter, so it is no promise for every hour.

horizon.title: How far ahead does it reach?
horizon.body: The forecast covers the next 60 days. After that the outlook runs to {date} with a wider error. Past it, a day shows the same weekday last year as we measured it, and says “last year”.
horizon.bodyNoDate: The forecast covers the next 60 days. After that the outlook runs on with a wider error. Past it, a day shows the same weekday last year as we measured it, and says “last year”.

error.title: How close does it get?
error.body: The further ahead the day, the further off the forecast can be. Once you plan a trip, you'll find next to the result how many minutes the forecast for one ride on one day can be off. Waits are rounded to five minutes, so days within five minutes count as equal here, and each park's best days are a set, not a ranking.

travel.title: How are the drive times calculated?
travel.body: Each drive time is by car without traffic, to the car park. Magic Kingdom's car park is the Transportation and Ticket Center, and the monorail or the ferry takes about another 15 minutes to the gate. For Volcano Bay you park in Universal's garages and take the shuttle, about another 15 minutes. Map data: {attribution}.

character.body: Parky rides roller coasters, yawns when nothing happens and has plenty more up its sleeve. It shows you a few of its tricks here; the rest you will come across as you browse.

data.title: What happens to your questions
data.body: Parky answers with the language model Claude by Anthropic. We store your questions without an IP address and delete them after 7 days. Parky only sees your location if you share it in the chat.
data.link: Everything else is in the privacy policy.

items.question: Does Parky cost anything?
items.answer: No. Parky is free and needs no account, just like the rest of park.fan.

items.question: Where do Parky’s answers come from?
items.answer: From park.fan’s live data: wait times, opening hours, forecasts, weather and our posts. It looks things up again for every question instead of remembering them.

items.question: Can Parky get things wrong?
items.answer: Yes. A language model writes the answers, and it slips up now and then. The numbers on the cards in the chat come straight from park.fan. If an answer looks odd, give it a thumbs down and we will take a look.

items.question: Why don’t I see Parky everywhere?
items.answer: Parky is not switched on for every visitor yet. The button on this page brings it along for your visit.

items.question: Which languages does Parky speak?
items.answer: All of park.fan’s languages: German, English, Dutch, French, Spanish and Italian. It answers in the language of the page you are on.

items.question: Can I make Parky quieter?
items.answer: Yes. Tap the ✕ in one of its speech bubbles and it stays quiet until the end of your visit. If “reduce motion” is on in your system, its animations stay off.
